notes:
Ideal gas equation

  • $PV = nRT = Nk_BT$ ($n$ = moles, $N$ = number of molecules, $k_B = R/N_A = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J K$^{-1}$).
  • Avogadro's number $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$. Gas laws are special cases: Boyle's ($T$ const, $PV=$const), Charles's ($P$ const, $V\propto T$), Gay-Lussac's ($V$ const, $P\propto T$).

Kinetic theory (assumptions & pressure)

  • Molecules are point masses in random motion, undergo elastic collisions, no intermolecular forces except during collision.
  • Pressure of a gas: $P = \dfrac13\dfrac{mN}{V}\overline{v^2} = \dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$ ($\rho$ = density, $\overline{v^2}$ = mean square speed).

Speeds of gas molecules

SpeedFormula
RMS speed$v_{rms}=\sqrt{\overline{v^2}} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m}$
Average speed$v_{avg} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$
Most probable speed$v_p = \sqrt{2RT/M}$
  • $v_{rms}:v_{avg}:v_p \approx 1.73:1.60:1.41$ (i.e. $v_{rms}>v_{avg}>v_p$). $v_{rms}\propto\sqrt T$ and $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt M$ at fixed $T$.

Kinetic energy & temperature

  • Average KE per molecule $=\dfrac32k_BT$ (translational only) — depends only on absolute temperature, not on mass or nature of gas.
  • KE per mole $=\dfrac32RT$; total internal energy of $n$ moles of monatomic ideal gas $U=\dfrac32nRT$.

Degrees of freedom & law of equipartition

  • Each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\tfrac12k_BT$ average energy per molecule.
  • Monatomic: 3 translational DOF, $U=\tfrac32nRT$. Diatomic (rigid, no vibration): 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5 DOF, $U=\tfrac52nRT$. With vibration, 2 more (KE+PE) DOF are added at high $T$.

Mean free path

  • $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,n\pi d^2}$ ($n$ = number density, $d$ = molecular diameter). $\lambda$ increases with decreasing pressure/density and increases with temperature at constant pressure (since $n\propto P/T$).

Exam tip

KCET typically asks 2 questions from this chapter — one on rms speed/KE numericals (often comparing two gases or temperatures) and one conceptual question on degrees of freedom or the ideal gas equation. Remember KE per molecule depends only on $T$, never on the type of gas.

questions.q: The equation of state for an ideal gas containing $n$ moles is
questions.explanation: Ideal gas equation: $PV=nRT$, combining Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws.
questions.trick: Memorise ideal gas equation $PV=nRT$ directly — combines Boyle's, Charles's, Avogadro's.

questions.q: At constant temperature, a gas of pressure $P$ and volume $V$ is compressed to volume $V/2$. Its new pressure is
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: $PV=$ constant, so halving $V$ doubles $P$.
questions.trick: Boyle's law: $PV=$const at fixed $T$ — halve $V$, double $P$.

questions.q: According to kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by a gas is given by $P=\dfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$. This shows that pressure is directly proportional to
options: the mean square speed of molecules (at fixed density)
questions.explanation: At a given density $\rho$, $P \propto \overline{v^2}$, the mean square speed of the gas molecules.
questions.trick: $P=\frac13\rho\overline{v^2}$ — at fixed density, pressure tracks mean square speed.

questions.q: The rms speed of gas molecules at absolute temperature $T$ is $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$. If the absolute temperature is made 4 times, the rms speed becomes
questions.explanation: $v_{rms}\propto\sqrt T$; quadrupling $T$ multiplies $v_{rms}$ by $\sqrt4=2$.
questions.trick: $v_{rms}\propto\sqrt T$ — quadruple $T$ gives $\sqrt4=2\times$ speed.

questions.q: At the same temperature, the ratio of rms speeds of hydrogen (M = 2 g/mol) and oxygen (M = 32 g/mol) molecules is
questions.explanation: $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt M$; ratio $=\sqrt{32/2}=\sqrt{16}=4$, so hydrogen:oxygen $=4:1$.
questions.trick: $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt M$ — ratio $=\sqrt{M_2/M_1}$, lighter gas is faster.

questions.q: The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at temperature $T$ is
questions.explanation: From kinetic theory, average translational KE per molecule $=\tfrac32k_BT$.
questions.trick: Memorise: average translational KE per molecule $=\frac32k_BT$.

questions.q: At the same temperature, samples of hydrogen and oxygen gas have molecules with
options: different kinetic energies and different rms speeds always in the same ratio as speeds
the same rms speed but different kinetic energies
the same average kinetic energy per molecule but different rms speeds
questions.explanation: Average KE per molecule $=\tfrac32k_BT$ depends only on temperature, so it is equal for both gases at the same $T$; however rms speeds differ since $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt M$ and the masses differ.
questions.trick: Same $T\Rightarrow$ same KE per molecule always; speeds differ via $1/\sqrt M$.

questions.q: The number of translational degrees of freedom of a monatomic gas molecule is
questions.explanation: A monatomic molecule (treated as a point mass) can move independently along 3 perpendicular axes, giving 3 translational degrees of freedom.
questions.trick: Monatomic = point mass moving in 3D $\Rightarrow$ 3 translational DOF only.

questions.q: For a rigid diatomic gas molecule (no vibration), the total number of degrees of freedom is
questions.explanation: 3 translational + 2 rotational (about the two axes perpendicular to the bond) = 5 degrees of freedom.
questions.trick: Rigid diatomic: 3 translational + 2 rotational $=5$ DOF — memorise this.

questions.q: Using the law of equipartition of energy, the internal energy of 1 mole of a rigid diatomic gas at temperature $T$ is
questions.explanation: Each of the 5 degrees of freedom contributes $\tfrac12RT$ per mole, giving $U=5\times\tfrac12RT=\tfrac52RT$.
questions.trick: Equipartition: $U=\frac f2RT$ per mole — plug $f=5$ for rigid diatomic.

questions.q: The mean free path of gas molecules $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,n\pi d^2}$. If the number density $n$ of the gas is doubled (temperature constant), the mean free path becomes
questions.explanation: $\lambda \propto 1/n$, so doubling the number density halves the mean free path.
questions.trick: $\lambda\propto1/n$ — double the number density, halve the mean free path.

questions.q: At a given pressure, as the temperature of a gas increases, its mean free path
questions.explanation: At constant pressure, number density $n=P/(k_BT)$ decreases as $T$ increases, and since $\lambda\propto1/n$, the mean free path increases.
questions.trick: At fixed $P$, $n=P/(k_BT)$ falls as $T$ rises $\Rightarrow\lambda\propto1/n$ increases.

questions.q: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic theory of gases?
options: Molecules attract each other strongly at all separations
The volume of molecules is comparable to the volume of the container
All molecules move with the same speed at a given instant
Collisions between molecules are perfectly elastic
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory assumes molecules undergo perfectly elastic collisions with each other and the walls, and are point masses with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces except during collision.
questions.trick: Kinetic theory core assumption: molecular collisions are perfectly elastic.

questions.q: Two gases at the same temperature have densities $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ and pressures $P_1$ and $P_2$ respectively. If $P_1=P_2$, then according to $P=\tfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$, the mean square speeds are related as $\rho_1\overline{v_1^2}=\rho_2\overline{v_2^2}$. This is consistent with rms speed being
options: inversely proportional to $\sqrt{\text{density}}$ at fixed pressure
questions.explanation: From $P=\tfrac13\rho v_{rms}^2$, at fixed $P$, $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3P/\rho}\propto1/\sqrt\rho$.
questions.trick: From $P=\frac13\rho v_{rms}^2$ at fixed $P$: $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt\rho$.

questions.q: A closed vessel contains a gas at 300 K. If the temperature is raised to 600 K without change in volume, the pressure of the gas
questions.explanation: At constant volume, $P\propto T$ (Gay-Lussac's law), so doubling absolute temperature doubles pressure.
questions.trick: Constant volume: $P\propto T$ (Gay-Lussac) — doubling $T$ doubles $P$.

questions.q: The value of the Boltzmann constant $k_B$ is approximately
questions.trick: Memorise $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}$ J K$^{-1}$ $=R/N_A$.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, at absolute zero temperature, according to kinetic theory the average kinetic energy of molecules is expected to be
questions.explanation: Since average KE $=\tfrac32k_BT$, at $T=0$ K the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules becomes zero (ignoring quantum effects), consistent with molecular motion ceasing at absolute zero.
questions.trick: KE $=\frac32k_BT\to0$ as $T\to0$ K — motion ceases at absolute zero.

questions.q: A vessel contains a mixture of two ideal gases at the same temperature. The average kinetic energy per molecule of the heavier gas compared to the lighter gas is
questions.explanation: Average KE per molecule $=\tfrac32k_BT$ depends only on the common temperature $T$, not on the molecular mass, so it is the same for both gases.
questions.trick: KE per molecule $=\frac32k_BT$ depends only on $T$, mass is irrelevant.

questions.q: Avogadro's number, the number of molecules (or atoms) present in one mole of any substance, is approximately
questions.explanation: By definition, one mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number, $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$, of elementary entities.
questions.trick: Memorise Avogadro's number $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$ per mole.

questions.q: The number of molecules present in 8 g of oxygen gas (molar mass 32 g mol$^{-1}$, $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$) is
questions.explanation: Moles $=8/32=0.25$; number of molecules $=0.25\times6.022\times10^{23}\approx1.5\times10^{23}$.
questions.trick: Moles $=$ mass/molar mass, then molecules $=$ moles $\times N_A$.

questions.q: The rms speed of nitrogen gas molecules ($M=28\times10^{-3}$ kg mol$^{-1}$) at 300 K ($R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) is approximately
questions.explanation: $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}=\sqrt{(3\times8.3\times300)/0.028}=\sqrt{266786}\approx517$ m/s.
questions.trick: $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}$ — convert molar mass to kg mol$^{-1}$ before plugging.

questions.q: At constant pressure, a gas of volume 2 L at 300 K is heated to 600 K. Its new volume is
questions.explanation: Charles's law: $V\propto T$ at constant pressure; doubling $T$ doubles $V$ to 4 L.
questions.trick: Charles's law: $V\propto T$ at constant $P$ — doubling $T$ doubles $V$.

questions.q: A container holds a mixture of two non-reacting ideal gases with partial pressures $2\times10^5$ Pa and $3\times10^5$ Pa. By Dalton's law of partial pressures, the total pressure exerted by the mixture is
questions.explanation: Dalton's law: total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures of each component gas: $2\times10^5+3\times10^5=5\times10^5$ Pa.
questions.trick: Dalton's law: total pressure $=$ sum of partial pressures, just add them.

questions.q: The van der Waals equation, $\left(P+\dfrac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V-nb)=nRT$, modifies the ideal gas equation to account for
options: the finite size of molecules (via $b$) and the attractive intermolecular forces between them (via $a$)
only the effect of gravity on gas molecules
the effect of the Earth's magnetic field on gas molecules
questions.explanation: The $b$ term corrects for the finite volume occupied by real molecules, and the $a/V^2$ term accounts for mutual attraction between molecules, both neglected in the ideal gas model.
questions.trick: Van der Waals: $b$ fixes molecule size, $a/V^2$ fixes intermolecular attraction.

questions.q: Graham's law of diffusion states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is
options: directly proportional to its molar mass
inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass
proportional to the square of its molar mass
questions.explanation: Graham's law: rate of diffusion $r\propto1/\sqrt M$, consistent with lighter molecules (higher rms speed) diffusing faster.
questions.trick: Graham's law: diffusion rate $\propto1/\sqrt M$ — lighter gas diffuses faster.

questions.q: Using Graham's law, the ratio of the rates of diffusion of hydrogen (M=2 g/mol) to oxygen (M=32 g/mol), under the same conditions, is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{r_{H_2}}{r_{O_2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{M_{O_2}}{M_{H_2}}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{32}{2}}=\sqrt{16}=4$, so the ratio is 4:1.
questions.trick: $r_1/r_2=\sqrt{M_2/M_1}$ (Graham's law) — square-root the mass ratio.

questions.q: A nonlinear polyatomic gas molecule (such as NH$_3$ or H$_2$O), which can translate along 3 axes and rotate about 3 independent axes, has a total of (ignoring vibration) how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: 3 translational + 3 rotational degrees of freedom (since a nonlinear molecule can rotate about all three axes) $=6$.
questions.trick: Nonlinear polyatomic: 3 translational + 3 rotational $=6$ DOF (all axes rotate).

questions.q: Using $\gamma=1+\dfrac2f$, for a gas whose molecules have $f=6$ degrees of freedom (a nonlinear polyatomic gas, ignoring vibration), the value of $\gamma=C_P/C_V$ is
questions.trick: $\gamma=1+2/f$ — plug degrees of freedom directly to get $\gamma$.

questions.q: The ratio of the average speed to the rms speed of gas molecules, $v_{avg}/v_{rms}$, using $v_{avg}=\sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$ and $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}$, is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{v_{avg}}{v_{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8/\pi}{3}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3\pi}}\approx\sqrt{0.849}\approx0.92$.
questions.trick: $v_{avg}/v_{rms}=\sqrt{8/(3\pi)}\approx0.92$ — a fixed numeric ratio, memorise.

questions.q: For a gas at a given temperature, the correct ordering of the three characteristic molecular speeds is
questions.explanation: Numerically $v_{rms}:v_{avg}:v_p\approx1.73:1.60:1.41$ (in units of $\sqrt{RT/M}$), so $v_{rms}$ is the largest and $v_p$ the smallest.
questions.trick: Memorise order: $v_{rms}>v_{avg}>v_p$ (1.73:1.60:1.41 in $\sqrt{RT/M}$ units).

questions.q: The most probable speed of oxygen gas molecules ($M=32\times10^{-3}$ kg mol$^{-1}$) at 300 K ($R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) is approximately
questions.explanation: $v_p=\sqrt{2RT/M}=\sqrt{(2\times8.3\times300)/0.032}=\sqrt{155625}\approx395$ m/s.
questions.trick: $v_p=\sqrt{2RT/M}$ — smallest of the three speed formulas, coefficient 2.

questions.q: A gas has pressure $1.5\times10^5$ Pa and density 1.2 kg m$^{-3}$. Using $P=\tfrac13\rho v_{rms}^2$, the rms speed of its molecules is approximately
questions.explanation: $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3P/\rho}=\sqrt{(3\times1.5\times10^5)/1.2}=\sqrt{375000}\approx612$ m/s.
questions.trick: $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3P/\rho}$ — direct from pressure-density kinetic theory relation.

questions.q: One of the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas is that
options: all molecules have exactly the same velocity vector at every instant
the actual volume of the molecules is negligible compared to the volume of the container
molecules exert strong attractive forces on each other at all times
the volume occupied by the molecules themselves is comparable to the volume of the container
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory treats gas molecules as point-like particles whose own volume is negligible compared to the container's volume — an assumption that breaks down for real gases at high pressure.
questions.trick: Kinetic theory assumption: molecular volume is negligible vs container volume.

questions.q: A real gas behaves most like an ideal gas, and deviates least from the ideal gas equation, under conditions of
questions.explanation: At low pressure (large intermolecular spacing) and high temperature (high kinetic energy relative to intermolecular attraction), the volume of the molecules and their mutual attractions become negligible, so real gas behaviour approaches ideal gas behaviour.
questions.trick: Real gas $\to$ ideal gas behaviour at low pressure and high temperature.

questions.q: A gas at pressure $1\times10^5$ Pa, volume 4 L and temperature 300 K is compressed to 2 L while its temperature is raised to 450 K. Using the combined gas law, its new pressure is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2} \Rightarrow P_2=\dfrac{P_1V_1T_2}{T_1V_2}=\dfrac{10^5\times4\times450}{300\times2}=3\times10^5$ Pa.
questions.trick: Combined gas law: $P_1V_1/T_1=P_2V_2/T_2$ — solve for the unknown $P_2$.

questions.q: At very high temperatures, a diatomic gas molecule can also vibrate along the bond, adding 2 more degrees of freedom (kinetic + potential) to the usual 5 (translational + rotational). The total number of degrees of freedom then becomes
questions.explanation: 3 translational + 2 rotational + 2 vibrational $=7$ degrees of freedom at sufficiently high temperature.
questions.trick: Add 2 vibrational DOF to rigid diatomic's 5 $\Rightarrow$ 7 DOF at high $T$.

questions.q: A gas occupies volume $1\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$ at pressure $1\times10^5$ Pa and temperature 300 K. Using $PV=Nk_BT$ ($k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}$ J K$^{-1}$), the number of molecules $N$ present is approximately
questions.trick: $N=PV/(k_BT)$ — rearrange $PV=Nk_BT$ and substitute directly.

questions.q: The law of equipartition of energy states that, in thermal equilibrium, the total energy of a system is distributed
options: equally among all the available degrees of freedom, each quadratic degree of freedom getting an average energy of $\tfrac12k_BT$ per molecule
unequally, with more energy going to heavier molecules
entirely as translational kinetic energy, regardless of the molecule's structure
only among the rotational degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: This is the statement of the equipartition theorem, which underlies the calculation of specific heats from the number of degrees of freedom.
questions.trick: Equipartition: each quadratic DOF gets exactly $\frac12k_BT$ average energy.

questions.q: At constant volume, when the temperature of a gas is increased, its pressure increases mainly because the gas molecules
options: start attracting the walls of the container more strongly
move faster on average and collide with the container walls more frequently and with a greater change in momentum per collision
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means higher average molecular speed; both the collision frequency with the walls and the momentum transferred per collision increase, raising the pressure, consistent with $P\propto T$ at constant volume.
questions.trick: Higher $T\Rightarrow$ faster molecules $\Rightarrow$ more frequent, harder wall collisions $\Rightarrow P$ up.

questions.q: At what temperature will the rms speed of oxygen gas molecules become twice its value at 300 K?
questions.explanation: $v_{rms}\propto\sqrt T$; to double $v_{rms}$, $T$ must increase by a factor of $2^2=4$: $T_2=4\times300=1200$ K.
questions.trick: $v_{rms}\propto\sqrt T$ — to double speed, need $T\times4$ (square the speed factor).
